title: Scribe or Press?
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Mediterranean Travels
description: A fixed-cost versus marginal-cost model of copying a 200-page book: predict the number of copies at which a printing press becomes cheaper than an ordinary copyist and than a master calligrapher, then move a slider to watch the cost lines cross.

educational.topic: Scribes, the printing press, fixed and marginal cost
learningObjectives: Calculate the number of copies at which printing a 200-page book becomes cheaper than copying it by hand, for an ordinary copyist and for a master calligrapher, predicting each crossover within one copy.

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Predict, then check with a parameter slider
keyQuestions: How many copies before the press is cheaper?
Why is the scribe cheaper for a single copy?
Why does slower, more beautiful handwriting make the press win sooner?
commonMisconceptions: The press was cheaper for every job, even a single copy.
The press's advantage was only speed, not cost per copy.
Making books more beautiful by hand always made them better value.
The cost of a press is mostly in running it, rather than in setting it up.
assessmentOpportunities: Predict the ordinary copyist's crossover (15 copies) within one copy in at most two tries.
Predict the master calligrapher's crossover (4 copies) within one copy in at most two tries.
Compare the three costs at 200 copies.
